hops.title: How a tight collar can fool the baroreflex
hops.text: A stiff buttoned collar or a razor gliding across the neck can be enough to make some people with carotid sinus hypersensitivity lightheaded or faint. The outside pressure deforms the carotid sinus wall, and its stretch receptors fire faster up the glossopharyngeal nerve. The solitary nucleus reads that burst as a sudden jump in blood pressure and answers the way it always does. In clinical testing, that answer can be a heart pause of three seconds or longer, a drop in systolic pressure of 50 mmHg or more, or both. A stretch sensor simply cannot tell a pressure surge from a tight collar.

sources.citation: Kharsa A, Ahmed I, Wadhwa R. Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity. StatPearls Publishing (2025), PMID 32644485.
Ntusi NA, Coccia CB, Cupido BJ, Chin A. An approach to the clinical assessment and management of syncope in adults. S Afr Med J 105(8):690-693 (2015), PMID 26543940.

image.caption: In susceptible people, pressure on the carotid sinus from a tight collar can slow the heart or drop blood pressure.

hops.afterHeading: The slow setter: the kidney balances salt
hops.title: Blood pressure does not have to climb with age
hops.text: Many people in industrialized countries see blood pressure climb with age and take it for granted. A study published in 1975 reported blood pressure and 24-hour urine sodium from Yanomami villages in the Amazon rainforest, where people added no salt to their food. This lesson's worked example has the kidney excreting 150 mEq of sodium a day; the Yanomami men tested averaged about 1. Teenagers had higher pressure than young children, but pressure did not keep climbing through adulthood, and in the adults tested, the salt-saving hormones renin and aldosterone ran high. This one population suggests the climb is not inevitable, and salt may be part of the story.

sources.citation: Oliver WJ, Cohen EL, Neel JV. Blood pressure, sodium intake, and sodium related hormones in the Yanomamo Indians, a 'no-salt' culture. Circulation 52(1):146-151 (1975), PMID 1132118.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A tiny pinch of salt on a leaf placed beside a tall glass cup full of salt crystals on a wooden table.
image.caption: In Yanomami villages with almost no salt, blood pressure did not keep climbing through adulthood.

hops.title: How pit viper venom led to captopril
hops.text: In the 1960s, Brazilian pharmacologist Sérgio Ferreira studied the venom of Bothrops jararaca, a South American pit viper whose venom lowers blood pressure. He isolated factors from it that were later identified as small peptides that block angiotensin-converting enzyme, the enzyme that turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II. One of those venom peptides lowered blood pressure in people too, but it had to be given by injection. Chemists David Cushman and Miguel Ondetti used what the venom peptides revealed, plus a model of the enzyme's active site, to design captopril. A clue from snake venom led to the first blood-pressure pill that blocks ACE.

sources.citation: Sciani JM, Pimenta DC. The modular nature of bradykinin-potentiating peptides isolated from snake venoms. J Venom Anim Toxins Incl Trop Dis 23:45 (2017), PMC5657115.

audio.title: Tubas, pit vipers, and borrowed kidneys
audio.transcript:
Blood pressure control runs on two clocks. One reacts in a few heartbeats, and the other keeps slow salt accounts over days. Three true stories catch both clocks in the act.

First, picture ten tuba players in a Paris research clinic, in a study published in two thousand eight, each wired to a finger blood-pressure monitor. Researchers asked them to blow medium-loud notes for fifteen seconds at low, middle, and high pitches, and compared those notes with a clinical Valsalva strain. Air flows out against little resistance on a low note. A high note takes a much stronger push, and the players' circulation responded much as it does during a classic forty-millimeter-of-mercury Valsalva maneuver. The recordings showed all four Valsalva phases as the players started the high note, held it, and breathed again. As chest pressure slowed blood returning to the heart, systolic pressure fell by about twenty-four millimeters of mercury on average. Unloaded baroreceptors told the brainstem to step on the gas, and heart rate rose by twenty-four beats a minute at its average peak. Then the players breathed again. Blood flowed back into the heart while the vessels were still squeezed tight, and systolic pressure shot about thirty millimeters of mercury above baseline. The fast buffer was working flat out, right in the brass section.

The second story is about moving the slow clock, and it starts with a snake. In the nineteen sixties, Brazilian pharmacologist Sergio Ferreira studied the venom of the jararaca pit viper, a South American snake whose venom lowers blood pressure. Ferreira isolated factors from the venom that were later identified as small peptides that shut down angiotensin-converting enzyme, the enzyme that turns angiotensin one into angiotensin two. With less angiotensin two, small arteries can relax, and the kidneys let more sodium go at the same pressure, sliding the renal function curve to the left. One venom peptide lowered blood pressure in people, too, though it had to be given by injection. The venom peptides helped chemists David Cushman and Miguel Ondetti work out how to block the enzyme. They used those clues to design captopril, the first A C E inhibitor that works by mouth.

Finally, what can a kidney transplant tell us about how the body sets blood pressure over the long term? In nineteen eighty-three, doctors reported six patients whose essential hypertension had damaged their kidneys so badly that they needed transplants. Each received a kidney from a donor with normal blood pressure. After an average of four and a half years, all six had normal blood pressure, with evidence that damage to their hearts and the blood vessels of their eyes had reversed. The six then spent eleven days in a research hospital alongside six matched healthy volunteers. On average, their mean arterial pressure was ninety-two millimeters of mercury, against ninety-four for the volunteers, and both groups responded similarly when salt was cut and then added back. Six patients is a small group, but the message is striking. The tuba players show the baroreflex at work from beat to beat. The transplant patients show that a lasting change in blood pressure can follow a change of kidney.
